name: Rice (Paddy)
season: Kharif (main); Rabi in parts of the east and south
sowing_window: Nursery: late May–June. Transplanting: June–July (21–25 day old seedlings)
climate: Warm and humid. 22–32 °C ideal; growth stops below 10 °C and above 40 °C. Very sensitive to frost.
soil: Clay or clay-loam that holds water well and can retain 3–10 cm of standing water. Avoid highly sandy soils.
spacing: 20 x 15 cm (transplanted). 20 x 10 cm for short-duration varieties

fertilizer.notes: Apply full P and K plus one-third N. Mix well into puddled soil.
Top dress when the field is moist but not flooded to the brim.
Match with panicle initiation for maximum grain set.
Apply basally if leaves show khaira (brown rust-like spots on lower leaves).

irrigation.method: Continuous flooding or Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD)
tips: Keep 2–5 cm of water during establishment and flowering.
AWD: let the water drop to about 15 cm below the soil surface before re-flooding. Saves 20–30% water with little yield loss.
Drain the field 7–10 days before harvest so the soil firms up for the combine.
Shortage of water at flowering is the single most damaging stress — protect that stage first.

care: Level the field well. Uneven fields waste water and create patchy crop stands.
Puddle before transplanting to reduce percolation losses.
Keep the field weed-free for the first 30–40 days — this is the critical weed-free period.
Apply the last nitrogen dose before 60 days; late nitrogen invites pest attack and poor grain filling.
Use AWD and avoid burning straw to cut water use and greenhouse gases.
harvest_notes: Harvest when 80–85% of grains turn straw coloured and grain moisture is around 20–22%. Dry to 12–14% before storage.
tips: Add 5–10 t/ha of farmyard manure or green manure (dhaincha) before transplanting to cut fertiliser need.
Treat seed with a fungicide or hot water (52–54 °C for 10 min) to control seed-borne blast and bacterial blight.

name: Wheat
sowing_window: Late October – end of November (delayed sowing drops yield sharply)
climate: Cool and dry growing season. 15–25 °C is ideal; above 30 °C during grain filling cuts yield.
soil: Well-drained loam or clay-loam with good organic matter. Waterlogging is very harmful.

fertilizer.notes: Place seed and fertiliser using a seed drill for best efficiency.
The crown root initiation stage is the most critical irrigation.
Skip if the crop is lush and lodging risk is high.
Helps in soils with a history of zinc deficiency.

irrigation.method: Flood or sprinkler; 4–6 irrigations depending on soil and rainfall
tips: Crown root initiation is non-negotiable — a single missed irrigation here can cut yield by 20%.
Irrigate lightly and frequently on sandy soils; heavier and less often on clay.
Avoid irrigation during strong winds to prevent lodging.
Stop irrigation once the crop reaches the dough stage.

care: Sow on time — every week of delay after late November reduces yield by roughly 1–1.5%.
Use certified, treated seed and a seed drill for uniform depth.
Control Phalaris (gulli danda) and other weeds in the first 30–35 days.
Earth up slightly and avoid excess nitrogen to prevent lodging.
Watch for aphids during warm spells in February–March.
harvest_notes: Harvest at 14–16% grain moisture when the crop turns golden and grains are hard. Store only after drying to 12%.
tips: Residue retention or zero-till after rice saves water and improves soil health.
Never irrigate wheat right after a heavy rain — waterlogging in the first 30 days is a yield killer.

name: Maize (Corn)
season: Kharif, Rabi and Zaid (grown all year in the south)
sowing_window: Kharif: June–July. Rabi: October–November. Zaid (spring): January–February
climate: Warm. 21–30 °C ideal. Frost and waterlogging are damaging.
soil: Deep, well-drained sandy-loam to loam rich in organic matter.
spacing: 60 x 20 cm (grain), 75 x 20 cm for sweet corn

fertilizer.notes: Mix into the furrow before sowing.
Most important nitrogen split. Earth up along the rows.
Supports cob development.
Maize is quite responsive to zinc; watch for white bud.

irrigation.method: Furrow, ridge or sprinkler; avoid flooding the whorl
tips: Silking to grain filling is the thirstiest window — drought here causes poorly filled cobs.
Drain excess water within 24 hours; maize dies in stagnant water.
Drip with fertigation gives the best water and nutrient use efficiency.

care: Keep the crop weed-free up to 45 days; use atrazine pre-emergence plus one hand weeding.
Earth up at the knee-high stage to support the plant and control weeds.
Scout for fall armyworm in the whorl from 15 days after emergence.
Plant a border row or trap crop like napier to limit stem borer entry.
harvest_notes: Grain maize: harvest when husk dries and a black layer forms at the kernel base (moisture ~20%). Dry to 13% for storage.
tips: Rotate maize with a legume such as cowpea or groundnut to break pest cycles.
Green cobs (baby corn, sweet corn) can be harvested 3–4 weeks earlier for higher returns.

name: Pearl Millet (Bajra)
season: Kharif; also summer in some states
climate: Hot and dry. Tolerates 35–40 °C and low rainfall far better than most cereals.
soil: Light, sandy or sandy-loam soils with good drainage; tolerates low fertility.

fertilizer.notes: Drill into the seed zone.
Top dress after the first weeding.
Improves sandy soil's water holding capacity noticeably.

irrigation.method: Rainfed; protective irrigation in dry spells
tips: One protective irrigation at flowering can raise yield by 20–30% in a dry spell.
Never allow water to stand — bajra is very sensitive to waterlogging.
Mulching conserves moisture in light soils.

care: Thin seedlings to one plant per hill 12–15 days after emergence.
Keep the field weed-free for the first 30 days.
Grow downy mildew resistant hybrids in areas with a history of the disease.
Bird damage is common near harvest — use scarers or harvest promptly.
harvest_notes: Harvest when grains are hard and the earhead turns brown. Grain moisture should be around 15% at harvest.
tips: Bajra is a climate-resilient choice for low-rainfall, low-input land.
Its straw is high-quality fodder — factor that into your returns.

name: Cotton
sowing_window: April–June depending on region, after 75–100 mm of rain or a pre-sowing irrigation
climate: Warm, 21–30 °C. Needs a long frost-free season with plenty of sunshine.
soil: Deep black cotton soil (vertisol) or well-drained alluvial loam.
spacing: Bt cotton: 90 x 60 cm or 120 x 45 cm; desi cotton closer

fertilizer.notes: Apply in the furrow and cover with soil.
First top dressing.
Supports boll retention.
Corrects reddening and poor boll set.

tips: Flowering and boll formation are the most drought-sensitive stages.
In black soil, irrigate when the soil 15 cm deep feels dry — over watering causes vegetative growth and boll shedding.
Stop irrigation once bolls start bursting to help clean picking.
Never use flood irrigation in heavy black soil — it waterlogs and rots the roots.

care: Do not grow Bt cotton continuously in the same field; rotate with a non-Bt or another crop.
Follow the refuge row rule (20% non-Bt border) where advised to slow resistance.
Monitor pink bollworm with pheromone traps from the flowering stage.
Remove and destroy rosette flowers and affected bolls weekly.
Avoid excess nitrogen — it makes the crop attractive to sucking pests and delays maturity.
harvest_notes: Pick clean, dry cotton in the morning after dew dries. Pick every 8–10 days and keep different pickings separate.
tips: Deep summer ploughing exposes soil-borne pupae and reduces pest carry-over.
Hand destruction of pest-affected parts is cheaper and safer than repeated sprays.

name: Sugarcane
sowing_window: Spring planting February–March; Autumn planting September–October
harvest_window: 12–18 months after planting depending on the season
climate: Hot and humid, 20–35 °C. Very high water and nutrient demand.
soil: Deep, well-drained loam or clay-loam with high organic matter.
spacing: Row to row 90–120 cm; 3-bud setts end to end

fertilizer.notes: Place in furrows and cover before planting setts.
Split into two doses and earth up.
Apply with irrigation and earth up again.
Useful in calcareous soils where yellowing appears.

irrigation.method: Furrow irrigation, drip with fertigation, or subsurface drip
tips: The grand growth phase needs the most water — never let it stress here.
Trash mulching between rows conserves moisture and suppresses weeds.
Drip irrigation can save 40–50% water compared with flood and raises cane yield.
Avoid irrigation 20–30 days before harvest to raise sugar recovery.

care: Use disease-free setts and treat them with a fungicide plus hot water before planting.
Earth up at 90 and 150 days to prevent lodging and improve rooting.
Wrap and prop up lodged cane to keep it safe from pests and rats.
Grow a legume intercrop (sunhemp, cowpea) in the early stage for extra income and soil nitrogen.
harvest_notes: Harvest at 10–12 months in the tropics or 12–18 in the subtropics when brix is highest. Cut close to the ground and crush within 24 hours.
tips: Ratoon cropping after harvest saves planting cost if the ratoon is healthy.
Keep a border of a different crop to reduce pyrilla movement.

name: Groundnut (Peanut)
climate: Warm, 25–30 °C. Needs a well distributed 500–700 mm rainfall.
soil: Well-drained sandy loam or loamy sand, rich in calcium. Heavy clay makes pod harvesting hard.
spacing: 30 x 10 cm (bunch type), 45 x 15 cm (spreading type)

fertilizer.notes: Groundnut fixes its own nitrogen, so P and K matter more.
Apply near the base and cover — calcium is critical for pod filling.
Helps pegging and pod development.

irrigation.method: Furrow or sprinkler; drip is excellent for summer groundnut
tips: The pegging-to-pod-filling period decides yield — keep the soil moist but never soggy.
A dry spell at flowering causes huge flower drop and lowers pod set.
Light, frequent irrigation suits sandy soil better than heavy flooding.

care: Treat seed with a fungicide against collar rot and a suitable rhizobium culture.
Apply gypsum at flowering on light soils — it directly improves pod filling.
Earth up around the base at pegging so the pegs can enter the soil easily.
Do not disturb the crop during pegging and pod formation.
harvest_notes: Harvest when the inner shell shows a dark brown lining and leaves start yellowing. Dry pods to 8–9% moisture before storage.
tips: Groundnut improves soil nitrogen for the next crop — use it in rotation with cereals.
Aflatoxin risk rises with late harvest and poor drying; dry promptly and store dry.

name: Soybean
sowing_window: June–July with the onset of monsoon
soil: Well-drained loam or clay-loam with good organic matter; avoid waterlogged and highly saline soils.
spacing: 45 x 5 cm (broadcast with a seed drill) or 30 x 10 cm

fertilizer.notes: Soybean fixes nitrogen; emphasise P, K and sulphur.
Very high payback in soybean.
Improves pod set and seed weight.

irrigation.method: Rainfed in the kharif; check basin or sprinkler in the summer
tips: Drought at flowering and pod filling is the main cause of low soybean yield.
Provide drainage in a continuous wet spell — waterlogging for even 3–4 days causes yellowing and yield loss.
In summer, irrigate at 8–10 day intervals depending on soil type.

care: Sow with a seed drill in rows rather than broadcasting for a uniform stand.
Seed treatment with rhizobium and PSB is essential.
Keep the crop weed-free up to 40 days; use pre-emergence herbicide plus one weeding.
Harvest as soon as the pods turn brown to avoid pod shattering.
harvest_notes: Harvest when 95% of pods turn brown. Thresh at low moisture; dry seed to 10–12% for storage.
tips: Soybean is an excellent rotation crop before wheat or maize.
Avoid sowing soybean repeatedly on the same plot — buildup of soil pathogens.

name: Chickpea (Gram)
climate: Cool, dry winter, 15–25 °C. Sensitive to excess moisture and to high temperature at podding.
soil: Well-drained sandy loam to clay-loam. Tolerant of low fertility but not of waterlogging.

fertilizer.notes: Add rhizobium and PSB seed treatment for best results.
Only if the crop looks pale.
Helps fill pods when the season warms up.

irrigation.method: Light check-basin or sprinkler irrigation; highly sensitive to excess water
tips: One irrigation at pre-flowering and one at pod filling is usually enough.
Never allow standing water — chickpea dies within a few days of waterlogging.
Excess irrigation encourages vegetative growth and reduces pod set.

care: Treat seed with rhizobium and PSB cultures before sowing.
Use a wilt-resistant variety in fields with a history of chickpea wilt.
Keep the field free of weeds for the first 30–40 days.
Watch for Helicoverpa (pod borer) at flowering and podding — the crop's main enemy.
Avoid late sowing; it pushes pod filling into the hot season and reduces yield.
harvest_notes: Harvest when plants turn yellow-brown and pods rattle. Dry to 9–10% moisture and store with a bruchid-safe method.
tips: Chickpea leaves valuable nitrogen behind for the next crop.
Install pheromone traps for Helicoverpa monitoring from the flowering stage.

name: Mustard / Rapeseed
climate: Cool and dry, 10–25 °C. Very sensitive to heat at flowering and to waterlogging.
soil: Sandy loam to clay-loam with good drainage; tolerates mild salinity.

fertilizer.notes: Sulphur is essential for oil content — never skip it in oilseeds.
Top dress with the first irrigation.
Only if the crop is pale and the season is favourable.

tips: Two irrigations — one at pre-flowering and one at siliqua filling — give most of the benefit.
Avoid irrigation during strong winds, which causes severe lodging.
Drain excess water promptly; mustard suffers badly in waterlogged soil.

care: Sow on time; delayed sowing exposes flowering to heat and aphids.
Apply sulphur for oil content and aphid tolerance.
Control aphids early — they can destroy the crop at the flowering stage.
Thin the crop to the correct plant population 15–20 days after sowing.
Do not allow grazing by stray cattle, a common cause of poor stands.
harvest_notes: Harvest when 75% of siliquae turn yellow-brown, in the early morning to reduce shattering. Dry to 8% moisture.
tips: Grow a mustard border around wheat to trap aphids away from the main crop.
Mustard honeybee pollination raises yield — avoid spraying insecticide at flowering.

name: Tomato
sowing_window: Nursery 3–4 weeks before transplanting: Jun–Jul (kharif), Oct–Nov (rabi), Jan–Feb (summer)
harvest_window: 65–90 days after transplanting, picked over 6–10 weeks
climate: Warm, 20–27 °C ideal. Above 32 °C flower drop occurs; below 10 °C growth stalls.
soil: Well-drained sandy loam rich in organic matter; pH 6.0–7.0 preferred.
spacing: 60 x 45 cm (staked), 75 x 60 cm for indeterminate types

fertilizer.notes: Mix into the beds two weeks before transplanting.
First top dressing with irrigation.
Supports the first fruit set.
Prevents blossom end rot and improves fruit quality.

irrigation.method: Drip irrigation with mulch is ideal; furrow or sprinkler also used
tips: Water little and often — frequent light irrigation suits tomato better than heavy, infrequent soakings.
Keep moisture even — irregular watering causes fruit cracking and blossom end rot.
Drip plus plastic mulch saves 40% water and cuts weed and disease pressure.
Avoid overhead irrigation in the evening; wet foliage invites blight and leaf spot.
Mulch heavily to keep the root zone cool and moist.

care: Stake or trellis plants to keep fruit off the ground and reduce rot.
Prune side shoots on indeterminate varieties and remove the first truss if the plant is weak.
Rotate away from potato, chilli and brinjal for at least 2–3 years to break disease cycles.
Remove and destroy plants showing virus symptoms immediately.
Harvest at the correct stage for the market — breaker stage for distant markets, red ripe for local sale.
harvest_notes: Pick at breaker to pink stage for transport; avoid picking under the midday sun. Cool fruits rapidly.
tips: Use a grafted or resistant rootstock in nematode and bacterial wilt affected fields.
Install yellow sticky traps for whitefly and blue traps for thrips for early detection.

name: Potato
climate: Cool, 15–22 °C ideal for tuberisation. Above 30 °C tuber growth stops.
soil: Loose, well-drained sandy-loam rich in organic matter; cloddy or waterlogged soil gives misshapen tubers.
seed_rate: 2000–2500 kg/ha of healthy seed tubers (30–40 g each)

fertilizer.notes: Place in the ridge or apply before earthing up.
Earth up around the stems to keep tubers in the dark.
Improves tuber size and starch.

tips: Tuber bulking is the most water-critical stage — keep the ridge base moist throughout.
Stop irrigation 10–15 days before harvest so the skin sets.
Avoid the water touching the foliage; late blight spreads faster on wet leaves.
Never let the soil dry out completely during bulking — it causes knobby, cracked tubers.

care: Always use certified disease-free seed tubers and cut only if necessary.
Earth up correctly so no tubers are exposed to light, which causes greening.
Ridge planting improves drainage and reduces the spread of late blight through soil water.
Harvest when the haulm turns yellow and the skin does not rub off easily.
Avoid growing potato in the same field as tomato, chilli or brinjal.
harvest_notes: Harvest in dry weather when the skin sets. Cure in a cool dark place before storage. Store at 4–8 °C for table potatoes.
tips: A two-week dark cool curing period reduces storage losses a lot.
Keep a mummy (haulm cutting) schedule if you need early harvest for a better price.

name: Onion
sowing_window: Kharif: May–June nursery. Rabi: Oct–Nov nursery, transplant 6–8 weeks later
climate: Cool during growth, warm and dry at maturity. 15–25 °C for growth, 25–30 °C for bulb maturity.
soil: Well-drained sandy-loam or loam rich in organic matter; heavy soils produce deformed bulbs.
spacing: 15 x 10 cm on flat beds or 3 rows per 1.2 m bed
sowing_depth: 1–2 cm in the nursery; transplant at 8–10 cm spacing

fertilizer.notes: Mix well into the bed 2–3 weeks before planting.
Top dress with irrigation.
Supports bulb initiation.
Improves onion pungency, keeping quality and yield.

irrigation.method: Furrow or drip irrigation; sprinkler is convenient on light soils
tips: Keep the crop well watered during growth but never waterlogged.
Bulb development needs steady moisture — irregular watering causes split and thick-neck bulbs.
Stop irrigation 15–20 days before harvest to help the bulbs mature and cure.
Use drip fertigation for uniform bulbs and better water efficiency.

care: Transplant 6–8 week old, pencil-thick seedlings for uniform bulbs.
Keep the crop weed-free in the first 45 days; onions are poor competitors.
Stop nitrogen 30 days before harvest to improve bulb storage quality.
Harvest when 50–60% of the tops have fallen over, then cure in the field.
Cure bulbs in shade with tops on for 10–15 days before topping and storage.
harvest_notes: Lift the bulbs when 50–60% of the tops lodge. Cure, top, and store in a well-ventilated dry place.
tips: Proper curing at harvest is the single biggest factor in reducing storage rot.
Rotate away from garlic and other alliums for at least 3 years.

name: Chilli / Pepper
sowing_window: Kharif: May–June nursery. Rabi: Sep–Oct nursery. Transplant 4–6 weeks later
harvest_window: Picking starts 60–75 days after transplanting, over 4–6 months
climate: Warm and humid, 20–30 °C. Very sensitive to frost and to waterlogging.
soil: Well-drained sandy-loam to clay-loam rich in organic matter.

fertilizer.notes: Apply in the planting rows.
First top dressing.
Before flowering.
Keeps the plant bearing over a long season.

irrigation.method: Drip irrigation with mulch is best; furrow irrigation is risky for the roots
tips: Water stress at flowering causes heavy flower drop.
Avoid waterlogging at all costs — chilli wilt in wet soils is quick and fatal.
Drip plus mulch gives the best fruit quality and reduces anthracnose through splash control.

care: Raise seedlings on raised nursery beds with a cover to keep virus-carrying insects out.
Use yellow and blue sticky traps for whitefly and thrips monitoring.
Remove virus-infected plants early — there is no cure once the plant is infected.
Mulch to reduce soil splash, which spreads anthracnose.
Harvest green chilli for a quick market or allow full red colour for dry chilli.
harvest_notes: Pick green chilli at full size, or wait for full red colour for dry chilli. Use scissors to avoid damaging the plant.
expected_yield: Green chilli 15–25 t/ha; dry chilli 2–3 t/ha
tips: Thrips damage often looks like a virus; check for the insect before pulling plants out.
Ratoon the crop after the main harvest can give a second flush of fruit in some regions.

name: Banana
season: Planted all year; February–March and September–October are common
sowing_window: Feb–Mar or Sep–Oct for a favourable harvest window
climate: Warm and humid, 26–30 °C. Damaged by temperatures below 10 °C and by strong winds.
soil: Deep, well-drained loam rich in organic matter with good moisture retention.
seed_rate: 3000 tissue-culture plantlets or sword suckers per ha
sowing_depth: Plant the sucker 10–15 cm deep in a pit of 45 cm3

fertilizer.notes: Mix into the pit with soil.

fertilizer.dose: Urea 100 g + MOP 60 g per plant
fertilizer.notes: Split into monthly doses in a ring 30 cm from the plant.
Improves bunch weight and fruit quality.
Corrects leaf speckling and improves finger size.

irrigation.method: Basin, furrow or drip irrigation; drip with fertigation is best
tips: Banana has a shallow root system and needs frequent light irrigation.
Drip irrigation saves 40–60% water; fertigate weekly for best growth.
Keep the basin mulched with dry leaves or straw to reduce evaporation.
Avoid waterlogging — it invites panama wilt and root rot.

care: Remove all but one healthy sword sucker per mother plant to keep a tidy plant population.
Prop tall plants with bamboo stakes to protect against wind.
Remove dried leaves and pseudostem sheaths regularly to reduce disease carryover.
Use bunch covers and stem supports to protect the developing bunch from sunburn and pests.
Remove the male bud (denavelling) after all hands are set to direct food into the fruit.
harvest_notes: Harvest when fingers are plump and angularity is gone, at 75–80% maturity. Cut the bunch with a 15 cm stalk and handle without bruising.
tips: Tissue-culture plants are disease-free and uniform — worth the extra cost in disease-prone fields.
Never plant a new banana crop in a plot with a history of panama wilt without a 6–12 month break.

name: Brinjal (Eggplant)
sowing_window: Nursery: May–Jun (kharif), Oct–Nov (rabi), Jan (summer). Transplant 4–5 weeks later
harvest_window: Picking starts 60–70 days after transplanting, over 3–5 months
climate: Warm, 22–30 °C. Frost sensitive and stops growth below 15 °C.
soil: Well-drained sandy-loam to loam rich in organic matter.
spacing: 75 x 60 cm (long-duration hybrids), 60 x 45 cm (short types)

fertilizer.notes: Mix into the bed before planting.
First top dressing with irrigation.
Second top dressing.
Sustains fruit size over a long harvest period.

irrigation.method: Furrow or drip irrigation with mulch
tips: Keep the soil evenly moist; dry spells cause small, bitter fruit and heavy flower drop.
Mulching reduces soil splash and hence bacterial wilt and fruit rot.
Avoid waterlogging, which spreads bacterial wilt rapidly.

care: Rotate away from tomato, potato and chilli to break the bacterial wilt and nematode cycle.
Stake tall hybrids to keep fruit clean and above the soil.
Remove and destroy shoots damaged by shoot and fruit borer rather than spraying repeatedly.
Use a wilt-resistant variety in fields with a wilt history.
Harvest young, glossy fruit; over-mature fruit become seedy and lose market value.
harvest_notes: Harvest when the fruit is tender and glossy, before the seeds harden. Pick with a small stalk, every 5–7 days.
tips: Grafting brinjal onto a wilt-resistant rootstock is a very reliable way to survive bacterial wilt.
Use pheromone traps for shoot and fruit borer and remove infested shoots weekly.
